narrative:
Based on the assessment, the model estimated a 12% probability that you will fail your final year. While this may seem low, the school's policy requires remedial courses for any student whose risk exceeds 10%, which is why this decision applies to you.

Interestingly, the three factors that most influenced this prediction actually all worked in your favour, pushing toward passing rather than failing — yet their combined effect was not quite enough to bring your risk below the threshold.

The most influential factor was your history of past failures: you have none, which is a strong positive signal and the single biggest reason your risk is as low as it is. Most students not required to take remedial courses also have no past failures, so you are on par with them here.

The second factor was your reason for choosing this school — its reputation. This also slightly reduced your predicted risk, suggesting that students who choose a school deliberately tend to perform better.

Third, the quality of your family relationships, which you rated as good, further nudged the prediction toward passing. This aligns with the majority of students not required to take remedial courses, who also report good family relationships.

Despite these positive signals, your overall profile still places you just above the intervention threshold. The remedial courses are therefore a precautionary measure, not a judgment of your abilities.

You should engage fully with the remedial programme — given your strong foundations, this support could be exactly what ensures you finish the year successfully.
